I paid $50 rent to p4 and now have $802. I own three unmortgaged properties: ELECTRIC_COMPANY, KENTUCKY_AVENUE, and BOARDWALK. p1 has a dangerous orange monopoly with four houses on several properties. I am deciding which post-turn action to take.

p2 is nearly bankrupt with only $20. He owns a brown monopoly with four houses but has mortgaged all yellows and Indiana. p4 is in jail with a get-out-of-jail-free card and owns several properties.

p4 owns Park Place and I own Boardwalk, splitting the dark blue group. He also holds two railroads and the greens Pacific and Pennsylvania, but North Carolina is unowned. He must pay or use his get-out-of-jail-free card next turn if he fails to roll doubles.

I will keep Boardwalk to block p4's dark blues, retain Kentucky Avenue to block p2's reds, and avoid feeding p1.

I can afford a single orange hit. I will keep p2 alive and cripple him rather than let him bankrupt into p1. He sits on St James with four houses on the brown group. I am now weighing my post-turn options.

I am weighing trade offers from p1, p2, and p4. p2 is desperate with only $20 and mortgaged all his yellows, so breaking that monopoly would not help him build or pay rent. I will likely end my turn instead.

I am reconsidering trading with p2. If he bankrupts to p1, p1 would gain his yellows and browns. I could buy one of his mortgaged yellows cheaply to block that. He has $20 and may sell a mortgaged property for cash. I am calculating a fair offer.

p2 might still refuse to sell a yellow even with $20. He cannot unmortgage any yellow for about $143, so his monopoly is effectively dead until he raises enough cash for a house. I am checking exact rent values for the brown group.

I am now considering offering $50 to $100 cash for one of p2's mortgaged yellows. This would give him survival cash while blocking p1 from completing a yellow monopoly if p2 dies. I can propose the trade without wasting a turn, since the engine applies it and asks again if rejected. I am weighing whether this trade is worth the risk.

I have decided to trade. I will offer cash for one of p2's mortgaged yellows. This keeps him alive and cripples him. It also blocks p1 from completing a yellow monopoly if p2 later dies. If I do not buy, p1 could gain all three yellows and unmortgage them to build a second dangerous set.

p1 has $2046 and could unmortgage all three yellows for roughly $440 to build houses. Blocking that set is critical. I am calculating the exact offer amount, since p2 previously rejected $400 for an unmortgaged property and may still refuse on principle. He needs about $143 to unmortgage one yellow, or cash to survive his next roll from St James Place.

From St James Place, p2 would land on Tennessee Avenue next turn. That property costs $750 in rent with four houses, which he cannot afford with only $20 cash. He would bankrupt to p1 immediately.

The immediate orange threat is low. Rolling a 2 or 3 from St James Place lands on Tennessee Avenue for $750, which p2 cannot pay with only $20. The probability of that fatal roll is just 8.3%. He will likely survive the next turn and avoid bankruptcy to p1.

I will offer $150 to $200 cash for one of p2's mortgaged yellows. I will emphasize that he cannot unmortgage the set anyway and that p1 would claim it if he dies. Any yellow would break the monopoly. I am deciding which one to request.

Marvin Gardens is the most expensive mortgaged yellow, but rent does not matter without a monopoly. I will keep Boardwalk and may trade with p4 for something useful.

I will not trade with p4. Buying Park Place would leave me broke and vulnerable to orange rent. I will not trade with p1 either, since they hold all the power. I have no reason to mortgage now.

I am calculating the mortgage cushion needed to survive an orange rent hit. The three mortgaged properties provide $385 in collateral. With $802 cash, I can afford to spend roughly $200 on a trade while still covering an $800 orange rent.

I refined the trade offer. Spending $400 would leave me $13 short of an $800 orange rent hit, so I cannot afford that much cash outlay. The maximum safe trade amount is about $350, leaving roughly $452 in cash plus the $385 mortgage cushion to survive a New York rent.

The $400 offer failed because the property was unmortgaged. Now that it is mortgaged, a lower price may be more appealing. I am also reconsidering trading with p4 or p2 for Kentucky Avenue to block reds.

I have decided that trading with p2 for one of his mortgaged yellows is the highest-value move. Blocking p1 from completing a yellow monopoly is the most critical strategic decision. I am now weighing how to price the offer so he accepts, since he previously refused $400 on an unmortgaged property based on principle. With only $20 cash and no ability to unmortgage or build on those yellows, the emotional argument against breaking the monopoly may no longer hold.

I will offer only cash for one of p2's mortgaged yellows. I cannot trade Boardwalk, Kentucky Avenue, or Electric Company without creating a red monopoly threat.

I will offer $250 cash for one of p2's mortgaged yellows. I am deciding between Atlantic and Marvin Gardens, but any single yellow is enough to block p1 from completing the set.

A bankruptcy transfer would give all of p2's properties to p1, so I must acquire one yellow before that happens. The $250 offer is survival cash for his next roll, and he cannot unmortgage the remaining yellows anyway because he lacks both the cash and the ability to build.

I will raise the offer to $300. That leaves me $502 in cash plus the $385 mortgage cushion, giving a comfortable buffer above the $800 orange rent. A $350 offer would leave only a $37 margin.

I am calculating my next roll from Pennsylvania Railroad. The most dangerous landings are Tennessee Avenue at $750 and New York Avenue at $800. I will also pass by Indiana, Atlantic, Ventnor, and Water Works.

I am now calculating the exact financial impact of spending $300 on a trade. A Tennessee Avenue rent of $750 would leave me with only $52 cash, which I could cover by mortgaging my three properties for roughly $385. A New York Avenue rent of $800 would leave me with just $2 and no unmortgaged properties. Without the trade, I would survive an $800 hit but retain all my assets.

I am now calculating how quickly p2 can raise cash. He has four houses on Mediterranean and Baltic Avenues that he could sell for $200, plus a mortgage on the Reading Railroad. That gives him roughly $300 in liquid assets. This makes a bankruptcy to p1 less likely than I had assumed.

The immediate orange threat is only about 8%, but it will fade once he moves past those spaces. The yellow transfer risk remains real but is not urgent.

P2 will likely survive a full orbit past the orange spaces, so buying a yellow now is insurance rather than urgent. I am lowering my offer to $100–$150 cash. That leaves me $652 and preserves more of my buffer against an orange rent hit.

I will frame the offer around rent insurance and the risk of bankruptcy. I will emphasize that p2 cannot unmortgage or build the yellow set anyway, so keeping two yellows and the browns is still viable. I am also considering a $200 offer as acceptable.

I have settled on offering $200 cash for p2's mortgaged Atlantic Avenue. I calculated the financial impact: surviving a New York Avenue rent would require mortgaging all three of my properties, leaving me with roughly $187 in cash and no unmortgaged holdings. A Tennessee Avenue hit would leave me with about $37 and Boardwalk. The 8% chance of an orange rent hit is low, but blocking p1 from completing a second yellow monopoly could be the deciding factor. I am considering raising the offer to $250 to improve acceptance.

I will start the offer at $150–$200 and raise it if rejected. I am now checking the trade schema.

I am choosing between Atlantic Avenue and Marvin Gardens for the trade request. I will ask for the higher-value Marvin Gardens, which would be hardest for p2 to unmortgage.

I realized that selling a mortgaged property to me for $200 would actually profit p2. He already received the $140 mortgage cash from the bank, so he would gain an extra $60 in cash while keeping the property. This makes the trade offer less appealing than I had assumed.

The trade is legal. I only need to pay $200 cash to acquire the mortgaged property and block the set. I do not need to unmortgage it immediately.

I will keep the public message persuasive but not desperate, and avoid revealing my orange rent fear or maximum price. I am also weighing whether to end the turn instead of proposing a trade. Lowering the offer from $400 could seem like lowballing and annoy p2.

I am reconsidering the $200 offer. A mortgaged property has only about $120 in remaining equity, so paying $200 for it may look exploitative and cause p2 to reject out of spite. I will raise the offer to $250 instead, which is generous for a mortgaged deed.

I will frame the offer as $250 cash on top of the $130 already received from the mortgage, totaling roughly $380 for a $260 deed. I am now considering whether p2 might accept a lower price if he is desperate for cash.

I will start the offer at $200 and raise it only if rejected. AI players cannot counter in the same action, so a rejection would not reveal their price. I should offer a price likely to be accepted rather than lowballing. The previous rejection was based on principle, not price.

I will offer $300 cash for p2's mortgaged yellow. This leaves me $502 in cash and $385 in mortgage cushion. A New York Avenue rent would require mortgaging all three properties, leaving roughly $87. A Tennessee Avenue hit would need mortgaging Electric Company and Kentucky Avenue plus part of Boardwalk. Both are survivable given the strategic value.

The absolute maximum I am willing to pay is $350. That leaves only a $37 buffer.

I will ask for Marvin Gardens, the highest-rent yellow and the best anchor to block p1. I am framing the offer around the fact that p2 cannot rebuild the set while mortgaged and holding only $20 cash, so selling one lot is the only way to stop p1 from inheriting a built monopoly.

I will propose the trade now. I will frame it as a mutual survival move against p1, not as a desperate request.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I have $802 and three unmortgaged properties. p1 has a dangerous orange monopoly with four houses and $2,046 cash. p2 is broke and mortgaged all yellows to pay p1's rent.

p4 is in jail with a get-out-of-jail card and $211 cash. p2 has a brown monopoly with four houses on Med and Baltic, plus Reading RR, but is essentially broke after mortgaging all yellows. Several greens are unowned, including Virginia Ave, Illinois Ave, and NC Ave. I just paid $50 rent at Pennsylvania Railroad.

I mapped the board from Pennsylvania Railroad. St. James Place, Tennessee Avenue, and New York Avenue are all owned by p1 with four houses. Indiana Avenue, Atlantic Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, and Marvin Gardens are mortgaged by p2. Illinois Avenue, B.O. Railroad, and North Carolina Avenue are unowned.

The next roll from Pennsylvania Railroad has roughly a 22% chance of hitting p1's orange properties. A $750 or $800 hit would leave me with only $52 or $2 cash, so I could survive without mortgaging but barely.

I will keep Boardwalk to block p4's dark blue monopoly and hold Kentucky to block p2's reds. I should not feed p1. I will mortgage only if debt forces it, and cash is my survival asset.

I am weighing a trade with p4 for Park Place to complete the dark blue monopoly. That would be powerful, but building houses on those properties costs $200 each and I only have $802.

Building one house on each dark blue property would cost $400 and leave only $402, which is still too little to survive an orange rent. p4 will not trade Park Place for Boardwalk, and completing the monopoly without houses is weak because unimproved rent is only doubled.

p2 previously rejected a $400 offer for Atlantic Avenue. All yellows are now mortgaged, so buying one would require paying the mortgage to unmortgage it.

Breaking p2's yellow monopoly would prevent p1 from claiming a second set if p2 goes bankrupt. p2 still has $20 and four houses on their browns, so they may survive for a few more turns.

I am now calculating the exact cost to acquire p2's mortgaged Atlantic Avenue. The purchase price plus 10% interest and the mortgage would total roughly $143, on top of the $400 I previously offered for the unmortgaged property. I am weighing whether that cash outlay is worth blocking p1 from claiming a second yellow monopoly.

I can afford to spend roughly $300 on a mortgaged yellow without losing my orange rent safety net. My mortgage cushion of $385 plus the remaining cash would still cover a $800 hit. p2 may not go bankrupt immediately since their brown properties can still collect rent. I am now considering trading with p1.

Trading with p1 would help them more than me, so I will not offer Boardwalk or Kentucky to them. I will not mortgage anything preemptively because that reduces income and costs 10% to unmortgage. I am now looking for a positive expected-value trade, possibly with p2 who is desperate.

I will not overpay for p2's mortgaged yellows. They would demand a large cash sum to give up their monopoly permanently.

I am now considering trading for Pennsylvania Railroad with p4 to reduce my rent exposure, since I just paid $50 there.

No trade is clearly positive expected value right now. I will end the turn.

I am now considering a trade with p2 for one mortgaged yellow at a low price. If I pay $100 to $150 for mortgaged Atlantic Avenue, p2 would receive the cash they desperately need while I block their yellow monopoly. After that purchase, I would still have roughly $652 in cash plus my $385 mortgage cushion, which is enough to survive an orange rent hit.

Mortgaging to pay rent would temporarily lose Electric Company income and the Kentucky Avenue blocker. p2 is unlikely to accept $150 for mortgaged Atlantic after rejecting $400 for the unmortgaged property. Repeated offers could waste trade exchanges and signal weakness, letting p2 extract more later or trade yellows to p4 or p1 for cash.

I am now framing the trade with p2 as a mutual survival deal. I would offer cash for one mortgaged yellow, giving p2 $200 to survive while blocking p1 from claiming a second yellow monopoly. This is more generous than my previous $400 offer because the property is now mortgaged.

A mortgaged property purchased for $200 would sit dead until I pay the $143 mortgage to unmortgage it. The strategic value is purely blocking p1 from claiming the set, not generating rent. If p1 later acquires the yellows, they would face the same $143 unmortgage cost plus building expenses.

Unmortgaging all yellows would cost roughly $561 plus building expenses. p1 has $2,046, so they can afford to do it. Yellow three-house rent is brutal at $550–$800, and with their orange set already in place, p1 would likely win the game if they acquire the yellows. Blocking them now is extremely high value. p2 is on St. James Place with only $20 cash; they must roll around the board before the next turn.

p2 is on St. James Place with only $20 cash. Their next roll would hit Tennessee Avenue ($750) and New York Avenue ($800), both owned by p1. They could sell their four houses on Med and Baltic to raise cash, since each house sells for $25.

Selling all eight houses would raise only $200. Adding the mortgaged brown properties and Reading Railroad yields roughly $380 total, still short of the $750 rent. If p2 rolls a 2 or 3 from St. James Place, they would go bankrupt to p1 unless they trade first. The probability of hitting Tennessee or New York is about 3/36.

Only about 8% of rolls from St. James Place would immediately bankrupt p2 to p1. The rest are harmless or pay rent. That is not urgent enough to panic-buy a mortgaged yellow. My own next roll still carries roughly a 22% chance of a $750–$800 hit.
